analysis.one_liner: Exempts incumbent phone companies' new broadband networks from sharing and rate regulation, in exchange for a five-year build-out pledge.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on June 28, 2001, received no further action of any kind, and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1996 Telecom Act, incumbent local phone companies had to share parts of their networks with competitors. This bill would have lifted those requirements for new fiber lines and packet-switching gear used for broadband, and would have barred federal, state, and local regulators from setting rates on the retail broadband service those companies sell. In exchange, the carriers would have had to make broadband available to all their customers in a state within five years — but with a broad exemption whenever that was not 'economically feasible,' and enforcement that hinged on a competitor winning a complaint against a 'clear and convincing' standard. It would also have directed the FCC to strip away any rules that treated phone-company broadband differently from cable broadband.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main gainers were the incumbent Bell telephone companies (Verizon, SBC, BellSouth, Qwest and similar carriers). They would keep full control of — and pricing power over — their new fiber and packet-switched broadband networks, no longer required to lease them to competitors at regulated terms, with retail broadband rates exempt from all federal, state, and local regulation [S3]. The bill's build-out pledge gave them a public-interest rationale for the deregulation, though its exemptions and enforcement design made the pledge easy to avoid [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Incumbent carriers choosing to opt in would be freed from the section 251(c) network-sharing requirements for any optical fiber or similar facility serving residential customers, and for their packet-switching capability and the resale of advanced or high-speed Internet service [S3].
Retail broadband rates, terms, and conditions offered by an incumbent carrier or its affiliates would be exempt from all federal, state, and local regulation [S3].

As a trade-off, carriers would have to be capable of providing advanced service to all their in-state customers within five years, and lose the deregulation if they failed to meet the build-out deadline or were found to have willfully violated collocation and loop-provisioning rules [S3].
The bill's stated purposes were to accelerate broadband deployment and achieve 'deregulatory parity' — the findings argued broadband providers should be subject to little or no regulation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the costs would have fallen on competing phone companies and independent Internet service providers, which relied on guaranteed access to the incumbent carriers' networks under the 1996 Act; and on broadband subscribers, who would face unregulated retail pricing from carriers with rebuilt control over the only wire into the home. The build-out requirement could have extended service to some unserved areas, but the exemption for cases that are not 'technically and economically feasible' and a complaint process whose burden of proof fell on the competitor made that benefit uncertain [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Competing carriers, independent ISPs, and subscribers

drawbacks.text: The bill would have removed competitors' access to incumbent carriers' new fiber and packet-switched facilities — the facilities most likely to carry home broadband — while leaving the incumbents free to set retail broadband prices without any regulation [S3].

The enforcement design was one-sided: a competitor claiming noncompliance bore the burden of proof under a 'clear and convincing evidence' standard and had to show material harm to its own ability to compete, and a state's failure to act within 90 days on a carrier's reinstatement petition was deemed a finding of full compliance [S3].

The five-year build-out promise contained a blanket exemption wherever providing service was not 'both technically and economically feasible,' giving carriers a wide escape hatch from the bill's main public benefit [S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledged it was responding to an asymmetry — cable broadband faced little regulation while phone-company broadband did — and its remedy was to deregulate the phone side; the bill itself directed the FCC to eliminate regulatory disparities within a year, which could have meant removing consumer protections on either side rather than adding any [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade — deregulation now in exchange for a build-out later — was weighted toward the carriers. The build-out promise came with an economic-feasibility exemption, and the only enforcement path required a competitor to win a complaint under a 'clear and convincing' standard, with silence from the state counting as compliance. Deregulatory parity with cable was a real argument: cable broadband was largely unregulated, and unequal rules could distort investment. But the bill addressed that asymmetry only by removing obligations on the phone side, not by adding any consumer protection to either, and it dismantled the network-sharing regime that had let independent ISPs and competitive carriers reach customers over the incumbent's wire.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee on day one, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Sam Brownback introduced the bill on June 28, 2001, for himself and Sen. Enzi, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1].
The action history records no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor action after the referral [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Republicans, in a Senate with 49 Republicans and 49 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Competitive phone companies and independent Internet service providers came out ahead by default: the network-sharing obligations the bill would have lifted for new broadband facilities remained in place, and the incumbent Bell carriers gained nothing from the deregulation they had sought. Broadband subscribers likewise kept whatever protections the existing regulatory framework provided, since nothing was enacted in this Congress on this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Competing carriers and independent ISPs, by default

for.name: Sen. Sam Brownback
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 2 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators signed on.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Fritz Hollings
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (after June 2001)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or hearing; as chairman he publicly opposed deregulating the Bell companies' broadband networks during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support came from three Republicans (the sponsor and two cosponsors), and no Democrat or independent is recorded as supporting or opposing the bill.

industries.industry: Incumbent local telephone companies (the Bell companies)
industries.note: The bill would have exempted their new fiber and packet-switched broadband facilities from the 1996 Act's network-sharing rules and from all rate regulation, letting them keep rivals off their newest networks and set retail broadband prices freely. The five-year build-out pledge was the price, but its exemptions and complaint-based enforcement limited its bite.

industries.industry: Competitive local carriers and independent Internet service providers
industries.note: These companies depended on leasing elements of the incumbent networks under section 251(c) to reach customers; the bill would have removed those rights for fiber and packet-switched broadband and made them the complainants, with the burden of proof, in any enforcement action.

The bill's 'regulatory parity' provision directed the FCC to eliminate rules treating phone-company and cable broadband differently within a year; cable faced little broadband regulation at the time, so parity would likely have ratified cable's lighter treatment while exposing phone companies to unregulated cable competition.
